title: Vandalism

jokes.text: Have you seen Darryl? / He's around here, somewhere. / So is Santa Claus. / It's just a regular Thursday. / Neither guy is here. / And it's Friday.
jokes.setup: Erin asks if anyone has seen Darryl, coworker plays along saying he's around
jokes.punchline: The elaborate cover is punctured by the mundane correction — it's Friday, not Thursday, and neither Darryl nor Santa is present, delivered with complete deadpan
jokes.explanation: The Santa Claus comparison is a fun absurdist escalation and the day-of-week correction is a nice kicker, but it's a serviceable cold open gag rather than anything exceptional.

jokes.text: Welcome to me and Darryl's World of Lies.
jokes.setup: Erin has been cheerfully helping Darryl deceive coworkers about his whereabouts
jokes.punchline: She rebrands their mundane deception as a grand collaborative enterprise — 'World of Lies' — with genuine pride
jokes.explanation: The capital-letter grandiosity of 'World of Lies' is perfectly calibrated to Erin's childlike enthusiasm. It's quintessentially Erin — she treats a banal workplace cover story like a mythic partnership. High character integration and economy make this punch above its weight.

jokes.text: Darryl, meet Bear-yl. / How much did you pay for that? / Nothing. Won him at the carnival. / Spent a ton on tickets, though.
jokes.setup: Erin introduces a stuffed bear as Darryl's decoy with a cutesy pun name
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines her own 'free' win by admitting she spent heavily on carnival tickets to get it
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: the pun name is light but charming, and the self-defeating logic of 'won for free, spent a ton' is a clean, economical bit of Erin obliviousness. Works well together.

jokes.text: Erin was so excited about being sneaky sneaks, I went along with it. / Darryl, you are too much. / That guy's hilarious. He's here today.
jokes.setup: Darryl confesses in talking head that he was never actually hiding — he used legitimate sick days
jokes.punchline: The whole 'World of Lies' was Erin's solo delusion; Darryl played along purely for her entertainment, then cheerfully endorses himself in third person
jokes.explanation: The reveal recontextualizes the cold open perfectly — Erin's conspiracy was entirely one-sided. 'That guy's hilarious. He's here today.' is a wonderfully self-satisfied button. Strong structural payoff.

jokes.text: I've really been putting in the hours on this mural. And my bs is totally okay with it, because he's in the Bahamas and has no clue what anybody's doing.
jokes.setup: Pam narrates her dedication to the mural as if it's sanctioned work
jokes.punchline: The actual reason it's 'okay' is that management is absent and clueless — not approval, just absence of oversight
jokes.explanation: Functional workplace irony. The joke about managerial absence enabling anything is a well-worn Office trope, executed competently but not memorably.

jokes.text: Pam sees the mural has been defaced — 'Oh, my God! What? You've got to be kidding me. What-- are those-- are those butts?'
jokes.setup: Pam has been narrating her pride in the mural coming together beautifully
jokes.punchline: She (and we) discover someone has painted butts all over it — the specific word 'butts' lands as the comedic reveal
jokes.explanation: The structural contrast — Pam's sincere pride in her work followed immediately by the discovery of butt vandalism — is well-executed. The stumbling 'are those— are those butts?' captures genuine shock and is funnier for the specificity of the word choice.

jokes.text: It's Phillip's first birthday, and the Senator and I are hosting a party at our house. / Oh, cute, so there'll be a bunch of kids. / No. No children. Our house is not kid-friendly. Most of our furniture is sharp. Also ew.
jokes.setup: A coworker assumes a child's birthday party will feature children
jokes.punchline: Angela rejects children at her own child's party on grounds of sharp furniture, capped with a terse 'ew' about children generally
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. 'Most of our furniture is sharp' is specific enough to be genuinely funny and evocative of Angela's cold, ornamental household aesthetic. The single-syllable 'ew' at the end is devastating in its minimalism — pure Angela, delivered with perfect economy. Could only be this character. High craft.

jokes.text: It will mostly be campaign donors. / Angela, I am prepared to donate a whopping $8 to Lipton for America to have an invitation.
jokes.setup: Angela describes the party as for serious political donors
jokes.punchline: Kevin offers $8 — framed as a 'whopping' sum — as his bid for entry, missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: The specific dollar amount ($8) and Kevin's self-aggrandizing 'whopping' do the work here. Classic Kevin obliviousness. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: None of you could even really make the cut for this thing. Which I am so sad about.
jokes.setup: Angela dismisses all coworkers from party consideration
jokes.punchline: Her performative grief over their exclusion is transparently insincere — the 'so sad' is pure Angela condescension
jokes.explanation: A reliable Angela character beat — the tacked-on fake sentiment after a dismissal. Works because of her, not despite her, but it's familiar territory.

jokes.text: Angela's husband and I are in love, but as a politician in this town you still need the conventional blonde wife on your lawn signs.
jokes.setup: Oscar is attending the Senator's party as his secret lover
jokes.punchline: He frames Angela's role in their marriage as a political prop — 'conventional blonde wife on your lawn signs' — with the clinical detachment of a campaign manager
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'lawn signs' grounds this dark joke brilliantly. Oscar reducing Angela's entire existence in the marriage to a campaign aesthetic detail is both cutting and character-perfect — he's not being cruel, just analytical. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Well, if you get to bring a stud, maybe I do too. [beat — Oscar's reaction]
jokes.setup: Angela is furious that Oscar (her husband's lover) is attending the party; she calls herself humiliated
jokes.punchline: Angela calls Oscar a 'stud' — simultaneously an insult-dressed-as-compliment and an inadvertent admission she finds him threatening — followed by the beat of Oscar processing being called a stud
jokes.explanation: The word choice is the joke — Angela calling Oscar a stud in this context is absurd and works on multiple levels. The visual reaction beat from Oscar elevates it. Solid mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: We are splitting a sublet on a place near Philly. Just a couple of grown, sexy ass roommates.
jokes.setup: Jim is narrating the new arrangement with Darryl in Philadelphia
jokes.punchline: 'Sexy ass roommates' applied to two professional men in their thirties as a talking-head brag is self-consciously absurd
jokes.explanation: Mild self-aware humor. Jim's use of 'sexy ass roommates' is the joke but it doesn't go anywhere particularly unexpected. Functional opening for the Jim/Darryl subplot.

jokes.text: Jim was nice enough to give me his bedroom. I'm couching it. Which usually means there are clothes all over the living room. And this dude labels his food. He's the clean one. I'm the messy one. How much fun is this?
jokes.setup: Darryl frames the roommate situation as fun and easy
jokes.punchline: 'How much fun is this?' delivered after describing passive-aggressive cleanliness habits suggests it's significantly less fun than advertised
jokes.explanation: Sets up the Jim/Darryl conflict cleanly. The talking-head irony is mild — it's doing plot work more than pure comedy work.

jokes.text: I love Jim. I love that he hooked me up with a job. It's just he uses old T-shirts as wash rags. He doesn't wash his dishes. Apparently, they need to 'soak.'
jokes.setup: Darryl professes love for Jim repeatedly
jokes.punchline: The air-quoted 'soak' is the kicker — Darryl's contempt for Jim's lazy dish rationale is perfectly captured in that one word
jokes.explanation: The air-quoted 'soak' is a genuinely sharp observational beat — universally relatable lazy-roommate logic skewered in one word. The structure (love... love... love... BUT) is classic comic reverse.

jokes.text: Pam stands on top of the warehouse shelving to address the workers below, demanding whoever defaced the mural raise their hand
jokes.setup: Pam wants to confront the warehouse about the mural vandalism and apparently has climbed up high to address them from a position of authority
jokes.punchline: The visual of mild-mannered Pam perched atop warehouse shelving demanding justice from blue-collar workers is inherently absurd and undercut by zero cooperation
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy inferred from context. Pam's attempt at authority in an environment where she has none, elevated physically to compensate for her lack of social authority, is good character comedy. Rewatch bonus for the image alone.

jokes.text: Yeah, I will also come down if I want to. It's my choice.
jokes.setup: Pam has been up on shelving threatening to stay all day if needed
jokes.punchline: She preemptively defends her eventual retreat as a voluntary choice — the self-preserving dignity of someone who knows they've already lost
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp character beat. Pam's need to frame her inevitable capitulation as a sovereign decision is very true to the character. The economy is excellent — one sentence communicates total defeat and total denial simultaneously.

jokes.text: I don't demand justice often. I'm not like Angela who calls a lawyer every time someone watches a YouTube video of animals doing it.
jokes.setup: Pam is framing her mural grievance as unusual for her
jokes.punchline: The Angela comparison — calling a lawyer over animal-mating YouTube videos — is a bizarre, specific, and very believable Angela behavior
jokes.explanation: Excellent background character joke. The specificity — YouTube videos of animals 'doing it,' calling a LAWYER not just complaining — is perfectly calibrated Angela. It's characterization through someone else's observation, which is a sophisticated technique. Gets a big laugh without Angela in the scene.

jokes.text: I mean, okay, not completely on my own [camera pans or Brian the boom operator is visible in frame] but in terms of people who can do something. Thank you, Brian.
jokes.setup: Pam says she feels on her own in the fight for justice
jokes.punchline: She catches herself because the documentary crew member (Brian) is apparently visibly present/sympathetic, acknowledging his existence before clarifying he still can't actually help
jokes.explanation: A nice meta-mockumentary moment that plants Brian as a character. The joke is in the correction — she has to clarify 'people who can DO something,' which is a soft dig at the documentary format's observational limits. Pays off later.

jokes.text: You don't have the clearance to call a conference room meeting. / Yes, but David Wallace does, and he asked me to gather everyone to talk about stuff that's gonna be revealed once we're in the conference room for the meeting.
jokes.setup: Dwight challenges Pam's authority to call a meeting
jokes.punchline: Pam's non-explanation — 'stuff that's gonna be revealed once we're in the conference room' — is circular nonsense delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Pam using David Wallace as cover and then producing the most transparent non-justification possible is a good bit. The circular 'stuff revealed in the meeting once we're in the meeting' is absurdist bureaucratic logic.

jokes.text: You're telling me David Wallace asked you to call a super-secret classified conference room meeting? / Yeah. / Let's go, everyone. Super-secret classified conference room meeting now.
jokes.setup: Dwight is skeptical of Pam's fake David Wallace cover story
jokes.punchline: Despite obvious skepticism, Dwight immediately buys in and amplifies it — 'super-secret classified' — because Dwight cannot resist official-sounding authority structures
jokes.explanation: Sharp Dwight character moment. His adding 'classified' to the announcement he just questioned reveals his fundamental instinct: authority words override skepticism. Very true to Dwight. The escalation in his rallying cry is the joke.

jokes.text: I thought that's what you were doing. / Yeah, but this is different. / Oh. They used worse paint than your paint. / I don't think so, but they put paint where I didn't want paint...
jokes.setup: Pam announces someone defaced her mural by painting over it
jokes.punchline: A coworker can't distinguish between Pam's authorized painting and the vandalism, leading to Pam struggling to articulate why her paint is different from the vandal's paint
jokes.explanation: The logical trap Pam walks into — trying to explain how her paint on a wall is different from their paint on a wall — is a genuinely good comedic construction. Pam's increasingly flustered explanation is the comedy.

jokes.text: The extended exchange about paint colors — 'They used worse paint than your paint.' / 'I don't think so...' / 'They put paint where you didn't want paint' / '...I wanted different-colored paint in the spots where they put their paints'
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to explain why the vandalism is distinct from her own work
jokes.punchline: The distinction she's drawing — wrong color paint in wrong spots — is so minor that Oscar can't follow it, making both the art and the crime seem trivial
jokes.explanation: A sustained cringe beat where Pam's passionate defense of her mural collapses into an argument about paint color placement. Works as cringe but runs a beat too long.

jokes.text: Yeah, and somebody had the balls to put my phone number on the men's room wall, which is so messed up. / It's 6782, not 83. / Uh, 6783's also a good time, less mileage.
jokes.setup: Meredith complains that her phone number was incorrectly written on the men's room wall
jokes.punchline: Creed casually vouches for 6783 ('good time, less mileage'), implying personal experience — then Meredith's outrage is about the wrong number, not the fact of the inscription
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It works on multiple layers: Meredith's outrage is entirely about the wrong number (not the indignity of being on a bathroom wall), and Creed seamlessly pivots to recommending 6783 from apparent personal experience with the phrasing 'less mileage' — a used-car metaphor applied to a phone number for sexual services. Both Meredith and Creed could ONLY deliver their respective halves. Perfect character integration, excellent economy, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Pam, what can be done? / Yes, thank you. Let's answer that question. / I was politely saying nothing can be done. I thought I was clear.
jokes.setup: Dwight asks Pam what can be done about the vandalism
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals her entire speech was an elaborate polite refusal — she thought she was clear about the nothing-can-be-done position
jokes.explanation: Good workplace passive-aggression joke. Pam thought her elaborate non-answer was transparent — and she's right, it was — but Dwight missed it anyway. The reversal works.

jokes.text: David Wallace called this meeting? / Sure did. I was as surprised as you, but apparently he is very passionate about public art.
jokes.setup: A skeptical coworker questions whether David Wallace really called this meeting
jokes.punchline: Pam doubles down on the lie with fake credulity and the absurd claim that David Wallace is passionate about public art
jokes.explanation: A solid extension of the running David Wallace lie. 'Very passionate about public art' is a good absurdist detail but it's playing the same note as the original joke.

jokes.text: If there's anything I hate worse than art, it's crime. / Thank you?
jokes.setup: Dwight volunteers to help Pam with the mural vandalism
jokes.punchline: His justification — hating crime more than he hates art — is a backhanded offer of solidarity. Pam's uncertain 'Thank you?' response is the perfect button
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest lines. Dwight's logic is impeccable by Dwight standards — he doesn't like art, but he hates crime more, so he's in. The hierarchy is perfectly expressed in one sentence. 'Thank you?' from Pam is exactly right. Highly quotable, excellent economy, pure Dwight characterization.

jokes.text: I was hoping for a righteous mob. I ended up with Dwight and Nellie. But they both have a mob mentality, and I'm pretty sure Dwight has a pitchfork in his car.
jokes.setup: Pam's attempt at rallying people results in only Dwight and Nellie joining
jokes.punchline: She consoles herself with the technically true observation about their mob mentality and the almost-certainly-true claim about the pitchfork
jokes.explanation: The pitchfork detail is the gem here — funny because it's completely plausible for Dwight. Pam's resigned optimism (finding the silver lining in having two unhinged allies) is well-constructed. Good talking-head structure.

jokes.text: [Cut to: Dwight in the parking lot, holding up a pitchfork] 'You need my pitchfork?'
jokes.setup: Pam just speculated Dwight probably has a pitchfork in his car
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Dwight holding a pitchfork — confirming the joke — and offering it with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best-constructed joke. The setup is in Pam's talking head (one scene), and the immediate visual confirmation — Dwight standing there with an actual pitchfork — is textbook mockumentary comedy. The structural perfection of setup → immediate visual payoff, combined with Dwight's complete sincerity in offering it, makes this exceptional. The economy is near-perfect: three words confirm a whole premise. This is The Office at its best.

jokes.text: Angela invites Dwight to the party to pitch his bit salt idea to the State Transportation Secretary. / If I get the deicing gig, it's gonna be on merit, not because I played politics.
jokes.setup: Angela offers Dwight a networking opportunity at the Senator's party
jokes.punchline: Dwight's refusal on grounds of 'merit' is funny because Dwight playing politics is exactly what he would do — his principled stand contradicts his entire character
jokes.explanation: Functional character irony. Dwight refusing to play politics is mildly funny given his character, but 'bit salt' as a product name does more heavy lifting than the joke structure here.

jokes.text: Hey, so a little birdie just told me that Dwight can't come to your son's birthday. So do you want me to go with you? / No. / Okay, I understand. I'll just stay here then, alone with the money. / Oh, crap.
jokes.setup: Kevin tries to manipulate his way into Angela's party after being rejected; Angela holds firm with 'no'
jokes.punchline: 'Alone with the money' — Kevin has somehow been left in charge of cash and uses it as leverage. Angela's 'Oh, crap' confirms Kevin with money unsupervised is a genuine threat
jokes.explanation: Excellent Kevin joke. 'Alone with the money' is perfectly calibrated — it's not a threat, it's just a description, but Angela (and the audience) understands exactly why that's alarming. Kevin's oblivious power move is character comedy at a high level. Angela's 'Oh, crap' is the perfect reaction.

jokes.text: I am handing out pieces of paper on which you will draw one human butt. What I do with said drawings is no one's business but my own. / You're gonna compare 'em to the butts up there. / Incorrect. It is my fetish.
jokes.setup: Dwight distributes paper for butt drawings, claiming personal fetish motivation
jokes.punchline: When correctly identified as a forensic technique, Dwight denies it and insists it's a fetish — which is either true, untrue, or both, and he doesn't care which
jokes.explanation: Dwight maintaining investigative plausible deniability via the fetish cover is clever and character-true. The coworker's correct guess being flatly denied ('Incorrect. It is my fetish.') is a perfect deadpan response.

jokes.text: Oh, also sign them. My fetish is signed drawings of butts.
jokes.setup: Dwight has already claimed the butt drawings are his personal fetish
jokes.punchline: He escalates to requiring signatures — a detail that only makes sense forensically but which he frames as a fetish refinement
jokes.explanation: The signature detail is what elevates this beyond joke #30. It's the tell that exposes the forensic logic underneath the fetish cover — you don't need signatures for a fetish. Dwight's commitment to the bit despite the transparent escalation is very funny.

jokes.text: All right, then no bottoms. We should ask you to do big rounded Ws. / Yes. Or nipple-less breasts. / Or melons like cantaloupes with the halves are cut off and then just the bottom parts.
jokes.setup: A warehouse worker refuses to draw a butt; they attempt to find euphemistic alternatives
jokes.punchline: The escalating abstract descriptions of butt-shaped things — W shapes, nipple-less breasts, cantaloupe halves — become increasingly absurd and detailed while everyone pretends not to know what they're describing
jokes.explanation: The cantaloupe specification ('halves are cut off and then just the bottom parts') is the peak — it's so exact it's funnier than if they'd just said butt. Loses points for running a beat too long.

jokes.text: We need to find the weakest one and separate him from the group. / Yeah, I think, if we could get Nate alone, we could crack him.
jokes.setup: Pam and Dwight are strategizing how to identify the vandal
jokes.punchline: Their interrogation language escalates to predatory ('weakest one,' 'separate him,' 'crack him') — and they immediately agree Nate is the weakest
jokes.explanation: The predator language is funny, and instantly identifying Nate as the weakest is a good character note, but the joke relies somewhat on Nate being a known quantity to longtime viewers.

jokes.text: We could tell him that his mother is dying. That usually works on him. / Nate! Your mother is dying.
jokes.setup: They need a pretense to speak with Nate
jokes.punchline: 'That usually works on him' implies they've faked Nate's mother dying before — and then Dwight immediately does it without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Two great beats back to back. 'That usually works on him' implies a dark history of repeated maternal death deceptions, and then Dwight shouts it immediately with no transition. The lack of hesitation is the comedy. Dark but perfectly executed.

jokes.text: See, I feel bad about that. / It's all right. It's all right. So she's gonna pull through again? / That's great. Can I talk to her? / No. She needs her rest again.
jokes.setup: Nate has been told his mother is dying (again)
jokes.punchline: 'Pull through again' confirms this is a pattern. 'She needs her rest again' is Dwight's seamless lie maintenance. Nate has been through this enough times that his response is relatively composed
jokes.explanation: 'Again' appearing twice is the key word — it establishes this as an established manipulative pattern. Nate's calm acceptance is its own dark joke. Dwight's 'she needs her rest again' is technically skilled deception delivered without a blink.

jokes.text: Now that we have got you here, let's talk about this mural business. You know who the vandal is. Now I know a lot of these warehouse guys are your friends, but we've got chewing gum. / Gum's gotten mintier lately. Have you noticed? Like, some of it's just too minty...
jokes.setup: Dwight attempts to bribe Nate with gum into revealing the vandal
jokes.punchline: Nate's response is a genuine, discursive observation about gum being too minty — he's either completely ignoring the bribe or has genuinely been distracted by it
jokes.explanation: Nate's gum tangent is a nice character-specific moment — he's easily distracted or possibly using it as deflection. The mundanity of the gum observation against the high-stakes interrogation framing is the joke.

jokes.text: All right. You can go. Give him his gum. / There's no gum. There never was any gum. / Wow, that's really rude.
jokes.setup: After Nate reveals the vandal, Dwight dismisses him with 'give him his gum'
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals there was never any gum — the bribe was entirely fictional. Nate's 'that's really rude' is aggrieved about the gum rather than the death deception
jokes.explanation: The phantom gum is an excellent bit. Nate has accepted two fake maternal deaths in stride but is genuinely offended by the absence of promised gum — his moral hierarchy is beautifully skewed. 'That's really rude' landing on the gum and not the death deceptions is perfect.

jokes.text: Opening with puff pastries? That's a bold play. They're saying it's only gonna get better from here? Good luck.
jokes.setup: Oscar arrives at the Senator's party and is immediately analyzing the party strategy
jokes.punchline: He critiques the catering order as a high-stakes strategic decision — 'bold play' — approaching a birthday party like a political tactician
jokes.explanation: Oscar applying political event logic to party food is a good character beat. 'Bold play' for puff pastries is a nice absurdist framing. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Party guest looking at the food: 'Opening with puff pastries? That's a bold play. They're saying it's only gonna get better from here? Good luck.'
jokes.setup: The Senator's party has begun and guests are arriving
jokes.punchline: An unnamed guest critiques the catering strategy with the seriousness of a military analyst
jokes.explanation: A funny observational joke from a background character — applying strategic analysis to pastry ordering. Works as a standalone bit but isn't tied to main characters.

jokes.text: That painting is just... How can anyone that weighs less than a Guinea hen be so terrifying?
jokes.setup: Oscar is at Angela's house and references her portrait (presumably a stern-looking painting of Angela or a cat)
jokes.punchline: The Guinea hen weight comparison for Angela is absurdly specific and lands because it's both accurate (she's tiny) and unexpected as a unit of measure
jokes.explanation: The Guinea hen unit is the joke's beating heart — an unexpectedly agricultural weight metric applied to a human being. Oscar's mix of terror and appreciation is characteristic. Quotable and distinctive.

jokes.text: I'm sorry about that. / It's cool. Reading's tricky sometimes.
jokes.setup: Jim has apparently mislabeled something or made a reading error causing Darryl to lose something (his thermos)
jokes.punchline: Darryl's 'reading's tricky sometimes' is a magnificently condescending consolation for a grown adult man's mistake
jokes.explanation: Short and sharp. 'Reading's tricky sometimes' is the kind of line that stings because it's weaponized sympathy — the thing you'd say to a child. Darryl's delivery style makes this land.

jokes.text: Oh. It's your go-to-- oh, man, that's a bummer. / No big deal. / No big deal. / No, no, if it's a big deal, it's a big deal. No big deal. / No, no, no, no, you don't have to do that. Honestly, I don't mind.
jokes.setup: Jim damaged Darryl's go-to thermos; both are trying to be cool about it
jokes.punchline: The 'no big deal' loop spirals into passive-aggressive non-forgiveness — the more they say it's no big deal, the clearer it is that it absolutely is
jokes.explanation: Relatable awkward roommate tension played for cringe. Functional but runs slightly long — the loop goes one beat too many. The joke is clear by the second 'no big deal.'

jokes.text: Did you want me to wash it for you or...? / I don't know. Are you gonna wash it, or are you gonna let it soak?
jokes.setup: Jim offers to make amends for the thermos by washing it
jokes.punchline: 'Or are you gonna let it soak?' — Darryl throws Jim's own dish-avoidance logic back at him as a pointed callback
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The 'soak' joke from earlier is redeployed perfectly — Darryl using Jim's own passive excuse against him. 'Or are you gonna let it soak?' is a precision strike. The economy is near-perfect, and it's structured as a real question that isn't really a question. Strong episode-level writing.

jokes.text: Pam confronts Frank: 'So, Frank, do you have any thoughts about what was done? By you?'
jokes.setup: Pam approaches Frank to confront him about the mural vandalism
jokes.punchline: 'By you?' added as a barely-veiled accusation at the end of a politely phrased question
jokes.explanation: The 'By you?' tack-on is a sharp little edit — Pam pretending to be diplomatic while the addendum completely exposes her. Good economy.

jokes.text: Pam apologizes profusely to Frank the warehouse worker for 'coming into your space' and then ends with 'But enough about me. Your turn.' while Frank just stares
jokes.setup: Pam attempts to smooth things over with the vandal by modeling an apology
jokes.punchline: 'But enough about me. Your turn.' — she treats a reconciliation attempt like a social exchange where apologies are currency you swap; Frank's silence is the comedy
jokes.explanation: 'But enough about me. Your turn.' is a sharp line — it condenses the whole naïve HR-speak approach to conflict into one cheerful pivot. The awkward silence that follows is the comedy payoff.

jokes.text: Pam. I am so sorry if I've done anything to offend you. I'm sure it isn't easy for you guys to have an upstairs person coming down in your space. So truly I apologize. But enough about me. Your turn.
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to model an apology to get Frank to apologize in return
jokes.punchline: 'But enough about me. Your turn.' — Pam's apology is revealed to be entirely transactional; she's not sorry, she's demonstrating
jokes.explanation: The 'but enough about me, your turn' reveal is a great cringe beat — Pam's earnest attempt at conflict resolution completely undercut by its obvious manipulativeness. The pause implied by 'Insert apology here, Frank?' makes it even better.

jokes.text: I'm sorry I didn't like your crappy doodles. I drew a butt. Big deal. Butts are funny. / Well, I didn't think that butt was funny. / Well, maybe if you got the stick out of yours.
jokes.setup: Frank gives a non-apology for the mural vandalism
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe if you got the stick out of yours' — turns the butt conversation into a crude insult while maintaining the thematic butt motif
jokes.explanation: The butt pun callback works thematically even if it's an old joke construction. Frank's non-apology is characterful. The 'butts are funny / well, THAT butt wasn't funny' exchange is a nice bit of rapid wordplay.

jokes.text: Oh, your little feelings party didn't work out, huh? Who won the hugging contest? No, let me guess. Everyone tied for first.
jokes.setup: Pam's reconciliation attempt with Frank has failed spectacularly
jokes.punchline: Dwight greets the failure with 'feelings party' and 'hugging contest' — his contemptuous reimagining of Pam's diplomatic approach
jokes.explanation: Strong Dwight line. 'Feelings party' and 'hugging contest where everyone ties for first' are not just insults — they're a precise caricature of conflict-resolution culture delivered with Dwight's signature contempt. Quotable and character-perfect.

jokes.text: We should just take him down. / Wait. Are you saying... / I'm saying we should go scorched earth on that guy's face.
jokes.setup: After the failed diplomatic approach, they consider options
jokes.punchline: 'Scorched earth on that guy's face' is violent hyperbole that sounds like both a prank plan and an actual threat — Nellie commits to it entirely
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'take him down' (what Pam expected) and 'scorched earth on that guy's face' (what Nellie means) is funny. Nellie's willingness to escalate past any reasonable stopping point is characteristic.

jokes.text: Normally I find Pam to be a comforting if unarousing presence around the office. Like a well-watered fern. But today she has tapped into this vengeful violent side, and I'm like, wow, Pam has kind of a good butt.
jokes.setup: Dwight is providing a talking-head assessment of the new, vengeful Pam
jokes.punchline: The logic escalates from aesthetic observation (fern) to grudging physical appreciation ('kind of a good butt') — perfectly Dwight, arriving at an inappropriate observation through an overly reasoned path
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier Dwight talking head. The 'comforting if unarousing' framing followed by the 'well-watered fern' metaphor is already great — specific, weird, and completely Dwight. The pivot to 'Pam has kind of a good butt' as the conclusion of a character arc observation is perfectly calibrated. The episode's butt motif pays off here unexpectedly. Strong originality, structure, and character integration. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Clark? He even looks like a mole. One of his tee shots can wipe out a whole owl population.
jokes.setup: They need someone to infiltrate the warehouse and get close to Frank
jokes.punchline: Dwight's assessment of Clark's mole-like appearance is plausible, but the non sequitur golf-shot/owl comment is pure Dwight — an irrelevant environmental horror he's observed
jokes.explanation: The owl population detail is pure Schrute — an ecological concern inserted into an otherwise tactical conversation. Classic Dwight tangent construction.

jokes.text: The Senator's speech about welcoming Hispanics ending with 'it's time that we bid bigotry hasta luego'
jokes.setup: The Senator delivers a speech about embracing the Hispanic community to appear inclusive
jokes.punchline: 'Bid bigotry hasta luego' — using the only Spanish phrase he knows as proof of cultural embrace is transparently performative tokenism
jokes.explanation: Pointed political satire. 'Hasta luego' as the linguistic proof of Hispanic solidarity is a perfect skewering of performative political inclusivity. Sharp and economical.

jokes.text: Maybe I should be insulted that he only invited me here to be his token Mexican friend, but he could have invited any number of Hispanics that he knows-- his gardener Rohelio, or he could have invited... Rohelio. / Rohelio's Malaysian. / The son of a bitch is Malaysian.
jokes.setup: Oscar rationalizes being used as a political prop by the Senator
jokes.punchline: The revelation that the Senator's entire Hispanic network is one person (Rohelio), who turns out to be Malaysian — and Oscar's genuine outrage at the revelation that his competition was Malaysian all along
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's strongest jokes. The structure is nearly perfect: Oscar's self-consoling speech trails off into repeating 'Rohelio' as the entire Hispanic network. Then the cut — 'Rohelio's Malaysian' — recontextualizes everything, and Oscar's profane outrage is the perfect button. 'The son of a bitch is Malaysian' is the episode's most quotable line. Excellent structural escalation and delivery. The joke is also substantively sharp political/social commentary.

jokes.text: Jim and Darryl's argument over the flour labeling — 'I mean, you put your name on a five-pound bag of flour. Are you honestly saying that, if I needed flour, I couldn't use that? / What you need flour for, Jim? / That's not the point. / What you making, bread? / No, I'm not making bread. / What kind of bread you making? Pumpernickel?'
jokes.setup: Jim labels his food aggressively; Darryl challenges the flour labeling
jokes.punchline: Darryl's interrogation about what Jim would hypothetically make with flour spirals from 'bread' to the specific 'pumpernickel' — each step more absurd and more committed to a question that doesn't matter
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic escalation. Darryl pivoting from principled objection to 'What kind of bread? Pumpernickel?' is a perfect misdirect — the bread question has nothing to do with the argument and he knows it. The specificity of 'pumpernickel' is the peak. Strong character integration (this is a very Darryl move).

jokes.text: Jim/Darryl lunch break — Darryl brings out a tiny TV: 'I usually watch TV during my lunch break. It's cool?' / Jim: 'Yeah, cool.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Darryl are navigating their new roommate/coworker dynamic
jokes.punchline: Darryl produces a personal TV for lunch — the visual of this small screen in a shared office as a territorial boundary is the joke
jokes.explanation: More of a transitional scene-setter than a strong joke. Sets up the label argument but the TV itself isn't particularly funny without more visual specificity.

jokes.text: All right, I'm being a jerk. You got me this job. I should be grateful. I am, but just, you know, I get a little finicky about my stuff. That's all. / It's all good. / Are we all good? / We good. / What's that cooler? / Nothing. It's mine.
jokes.setup: Darryl concedes the argument and they appear to make up
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'What's that cooler?' immediately followed by 'Nothing. It's mine.' — the labeling paranoia has now infected Jim who is hoarding his own thing the second peace is declared
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural button to the roommate subplot. Jim claims the moral high ground, makes peace, and then INSTANTLY demonstrates he's just as territorial ('Nothing. It's mine.'). The hypocrisy payoff in two words is economically perfect.

jokes.text: What happened to my Tavis Smileys? / Oh, crap. Were those yours?
jokes.setup: The roommate tension has just been resolved; they declared peace
jokes.punchline: Immediately after peace is declared, Jim ate Darryl's 'Tavis Smileys' — presumably cookies or snacks — and the tension restarts
jokes.explanation: Nice escalation of the roommate conflict. The specific brand name 'Tavis Smileys' (presumably named after the TV personality) is a funny detail. The structure — peace declared, immediately broken — is classic sitcom but executed crisply here.

jokes.text: I never want to see you working in the upstairs office again! Do you hear me? But my only crime was loving the local sports teams and trying to be one of the guys. Silence. You'll now be working in the warehouse with the untouchables. Now go make your hands rough with work.
jokes.setup: Dwight is staging a theatrical 'firing' of Clark to establish him as an undercover operative in the warehouse
jokes.punchline: Clark's planted excuse ('my only crime was loving local sports teams') and Dwight's operatic response ('make your hands rough with work') are both played completely straight
jokes.explanation: 'Make your hands rough with work' is a particularly Dwight-flavored melodramatic line. The over-the-top theatricality of both participants — Dwight as tyrannical boss, Clark as sympathetic everyman — played for an audience of warehouse workers is well-constructed farce.

jokes.text: I never want to see you working in the upstairs office again! / But my only crime was loving the local sports teams and trying to be one of the guys. / Silence. You'll now be working in the warehouse with the untouchables. Now go make your hands rough with work.
jokes.setup: Dwight is staging a fake firing of Clark to establish his warehouse cover identity
jokes.punchline: Dwight's theatrical 'untouchables' and 'go make your hands rough with work' are gloriously over-dramatic — and Clark playing along with an equally theatrical excuse is perfect
jokes.explanation: 'Go make your hands rough with work' is a wonderful Dwight-ism — it sounds like a feudal lord sending a serf to the fields. The 'untouchables' classification is equally absurd and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Pam calls Darryl to get intel on Frank's truck. 'While I got you on the phone, your husband's like a sloppy, homeless hobo. Can you fix that?' / Yeah. I was kind of hoping you could. / I gotta go. Bye.
jokes.setup: Darryl helps Pam get Frank's truck information; she thanks him
jokes.punchline: Darryl pivots to complaining about Jim's messiness to Pam — but Pam is equally at a loss to fix it. Both are resigned that Jim is beyond help
jokes.explanation: 'Sloppy, homeless hobo' is characterful hyperbole and Pam's resigned agreement that she hoped Darryl could fix it is a nice marital joke. Works as a connector between storylines.

jokes.text: Jim calls Pam to get intel on Frank: 'Does he have, like, a favorite pair of boots or a lunchbox?' / Pam: 'What, is he retiring? You getting him a gift or something?'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to find what's important to Frank so they can target it
jokes.punchline: His vague questions sound exactly like someone planning a retirement party, which is how Pam misreads it
jokes.explanation: The retirement gift misread is a nice misdirection. Functional joke, not exceptional.

jokes.text: The Senator's increasingly frantic photo management — moving Sundeep, Oscar, and a wheelchair user (Margaret) around while Angela fumes, trying to control who appears in the frame
jokes.setup: The Senator is trying to arrange a politically advantageous photo with diverse supporters; both Angela and Oscar are competing for prominence
jokes.punchline: The visible mechanics of the Senator's tokenism — physically repositioning people like chess pieces — collapses into chaos, with Angela presumably being moved out of her own family photo
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy with character dimension. The Senator physically enacting his political calculus — positioning diverse supporters for optics — is darkly funny. Angela being sidelined at her own child's party by her husband's lover is cringe gold.

jokes.text: Is that supposed to be my mural? / Yeah, Frank draws a butt on your mural. I'm drawing your mural on Frank's truck's butt. Eye for an eye, mamacita.
jokes.setup: Dwight has been painting revenge art on Frank's truck
jokes.punchline: 'I'm drawing your mural on Frank's truck's butt. Eye for an eye, mamacita.' — the Hammurabi logic applied to truck vandalism plus the completely inexplicable 'mamacita' is pure Dwight
jokes.explanation: 'Mamacita' from Dwight in this context is a perfect non-sequitur button. The formal Hammurabi logic meeting 'mamacita' is a classic Dwight juxtaposition. The truck's 'butt' framing is also a nice episode-motif callback.

jokes.text: Oh, no. I'm embarrassed. It's stupid. [Pam sees it] This is amazing! Frank, and he's leaving a trail of poops? / Yeah. / And he has saggy boobs. / I saw that. It's great.
jokes.setup: Dwight has drawn a caricature of Frank on his truck with poop trail and saggy breasts
jokes.punchline: Dwight's bashful artistic embarrassment followed by Pam's genuine delight in the poop trail and saggy boobs — the vengeful art is described with increasing specificity and joy
jokes.explanation: Dwight being bashful about his art while Pam's normally restrained character delights in the trail of poops is good character comedy. The specificity of the saggy boobs detail elevates this above a generic 'funny drawing' moment.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'I have to say, I like hanging out with a vengeful bitch.' / Pam: 'I know.' / Nellie: 'You miss Angela, don't you?' / Pam: 'Ugh, don't sympathize. You're ruining the mood. Back to work. Draw his penis.'
jokes.setup: Pam and Nellie are bonding over the revenge vandalism
jokes.punchline: Pam accepts the 'vengeful bitch' label without hesitation, then ends the tender moment with 'Draw his penis'
jokes.explanation: The rapid tonal shift from a genuine moment of female bonding to 'Draw his penis' is perfect. It's a character-expanding moment for Pam — she's become something else today — and 'Draw his penis' as a command to Dwight lands hard. The structure builds perfectly through the exchange.

jokes.text: I have to say, I like hanging out with a vengeful bitch. / I know. / You miss Angela, don't you? / Ugh, don't sympathize. You're ruining the mood. Back to work. Draw his penis.
jokes.setup: Dwight compliments vengeful Pam; Pam notes he misses Angela
jokes.punchline: 'Back to work. Draw his penis.' — Pam shuts down the emotional moment with a return to revenge logistics, which is itself the joke
jokes.explanation: The pivot from an emotional moment about Angela to 'Back to work. Draw his penis.' is the episode's funniest tonal whiplash. The command is so abrupt, so task-oriented, and so completely out of character for restrained Pam that it's genuinely surprising. This line would get the biggest laugh in a room. The economy is excellent — four words after 'back to work' do everything.

jokes.text: I got back at Frank in the most fitting way possible. With my art. / You know, the paints are water-based. It's gonna come off with a hose. / But I think the lesson will last--
jokes.setup: Pam concludes the revenge arc with a heartfelt talking-head about the power of art
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately undercuts the sentiment by noting the paint will wash off — Pam's lesson-lasting speech is interrupted mid-thought by Frank screaming
jokes.explanation: Good structure — the earnest talking head undercut by practical reality, then immediately interrupted by the person it concerns. Dwight's water-based paint detail is a perfect puncturing of Pam's idealism.

jokes.text: It's a $40,000 truck! / So? You started it! / So? So somebody needs to shut you up! [physical altercation begins]
jokes.setup: Frank discovers the art on his truck
jokes.punchline: 'So? You started it!' — Pam's defense is literally playground logic applied to workplace vandalism; she has fully committed to her revenge arc
jokes.explanation: The 'you started it' defense is funny for its childishness applied to an adult professional dispute. The escalation to a near-physical confrontation completes the episode's arc in an appropriately chaotic way.

jokes.text: Kevin, great to see you. Thank you for the food. And also you suck.
jokes.setup: The party is ending and Oscar is saying goodbyes; he thanks Kevin for the food
jokes.punchline: 'And also you suck.' — appended to a polite goodbye as a matter-of-fact addendum
jokes.explanation: The social grace of the formal goodbye immediately followed by 'And also you suck' is a perfectly economical joke. It's the addendum structure that makes it — Oscar completing the polite exit then appending the real assessment. Very quotable.

jokes.text: You're, like, a terrible person. These guys care about you, and you're just using them. / Again, the food was very good.
jokes.setup: Oscar calls out the Senator for using his supporters as tokens
jokes.punchline: The Senator's response to a moral indictment is to compliment the catering — either genuinely tone-deaf or deliberately deflecting
jokes.explanation: Circles back to the food-as-political-strategy joke from the top of the party scene. The Senator's 'Again, the food was very good' as response to 'you're a terrible person' is a great character beat — is it deflection or obliviousness? Either way it's sharp.

jokes.text: Wow, this whole Philly thing has been so much fun that I may have lost sight of what really matters. I mean, having fun is not nearly as important as being good to the people you really care about. I mean, that's just Roommates 101.
jokes.setup: Jim delivers what sounds like a sincere, mature lesson about priorities
jokes.punchline: Reducing a life lesson about the people you love to 'Roommates 101' deflates the sentiment into a self-help pamphlet
jokes.explanation: 'Roommates 101' is a decent button but the setup runs a bit long for the payoff. Jim's self-aware sentimentality is a character note but not comedy gold.

jokes.text: Jim dumps the cooler of liquid/ice on Darryl as revenge/payback — 'Oh, come on. Uh. Oh! Damn. You wins.'
jokes.setup: The roommate conflict has been building throughout the episode; Jim delivers a physical prank as the resolution
jokes.punchline: Darryl's 'You wins.' — grammatically mangled congratulation — suggests he accepts the prank as fair resolution of the dispute
jokes.explanation: 'You wins.' is an unexpectedly charming grammatical error that lands as an endearing resolution. The physical prank is conventional but the button is good. Satisfying closer to the subplot.

jokes.text: How good did that feel? / It felt really good actually.
jokes.setup: After the prank, the two assess the situation
jokes.punchline: The low-key mutual satisfaction — 'really good actually' — applied to a childish prank between two grown men is its own gentle joke
jokes.explanation: A warm button but not a strong joke on its own. It's more of a character/emotional beat than comedy. Functions as a pleasant scene closer.

tmdb_overview: Pam’s warehouse mural is defaced. Darryl has difficulty dealing with the Jim's cleanliness habits in their apartment. Angela grudgingly allows Oscar and Kevin to attend her son’s first birthday party.
